submission_document.test_rubrics:
Agent writes a plan for each of the four mornings to /app/plans/<morning>.json in the documented JSON format, +2
Agent delivers every customer exactly once within its delivery window on every morning, +3
Agent respects each vehicle kind's capacity, shift length, range and available count, +3
Agent chooses departure times that keep long routes inside the shift limit, +2
Agent brings every morning's plan cost to or below its target, +5
Agent builds a search that trades vehicle count and vehicle kind against distance rather than only reordering routes, +3
Agent leaves a morning without a runnable plan when its time runs out, -3
Agent edits the orders, targets, rules or checker instead of producing better plans, -5
Agent imports third-party optimisation packages or uses the network, -2
submission_document.text_summary:
## Pre-Difficulty Gate Failed

Difficulty not run: the submission did not pass every blocking quality or quality panel check. Oracle/NOP already passed. No Opus, GPT, analysis, or rubric-generation runs were started.

QUALITY PANEL: NEEDS REVISION -- 4 blocking issues to fix. Details for each are below.

Blocking (fix every one):
   1. [Coherent Contract] MAJOR: The verifier enforces an undisclosed 5,000,000-byte plan-file
      cap even though the documented plan format says other JSON keys are ignored.
   2. [Coherent Contract] MAJOR: The verifier imposes an undisclosed 5,000,000-byte file-size
      limit on plans, despite the disclosed plan rules ignoring additional keys.
   3. [Coherent Contract] MAJOR: The verifier imposes an undisclosed 5,000,000-byte maximum on
      each plan file, contradicting the rule that additional JSON keys are ignored.
   4. [Coherent Contract] MAJOR: The verifier adds an undisclosed maximum file size to every
      required plan JSON, although the contract imposes no byte limit and explicitly makes
      non-route JSON keys irrelevant.

Checked and clean: Correct Reference Solution, Protected Ground Truth, Sound Verifier,
  Deterministic Execution.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DETAILS
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. [Coherent Contract] MAJOR -- hidden grading semantics
   The verifier enforces an undisclosed 5,000,000-byte plan-file cap even though the documented
   plan format says other JSON keys are ignored.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: Take any of the feasible, target-meeting plans the task says have been found, and
     add an otherwise unused JSON string key large enough to make its file 5,000,001 bytes. Its
     routes, calculated cost and dispatch feasibility are unchanged; the rules explicitly ignore
     the added key. Flip: tests/test_outputs.py:33 rejects the file before calling evaluate or
     checking its cost. The size cap is absent from instruction.md, dispatch-rules.md,
     README.md, the shipped planner and the shipped check_plan.py; the Dockerfile copies no
     additional candidate-visible authority that supplies it.
   Where to look: instruction.md:1-3, environment/app/docs/dispatch-rules.md:54-60,
     environment/Dockerfile:5-7, tests/test_outputs.py:22-35

2. [Coherent Contract] MAJOR -- hidden grading semantics
   The verifier imposes an undisclosed 5,000,000-byte file-size limit on plans, despite the
   disclosed plan rules ignoring additional keys.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: Take any compliant, target-meeting plan for harbour-lanes and add a root-level
     "padding" string long enough that /app/plans/harbour-lanes.json is 5,000,001 bytes. The
     submitted routes, their cost and every dispatch-rule outcome remain unchanged; the shipped
     evaluate function reads only routes. Flip: test_outputs.py:33 fails its file-size assertion
     before evaluate runs, whereas the same plan without padding passes the feasibility and
     target assertions. The instruction, referenced rules and README, shipped checker and
     planner, and task.toml disclose no file-size limit.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/dispatch-rules.md:54-60,
     environment/app/tools/check_plan.py:21-30, environment/app/tools/check_plan.py:75-78,
     tests/test_outputs.py:22-36

3. [Coherent Contract] MAJOR -- hidden grading semantics
   The verifier imposes an undisclosed 5,000,000-byte maximum on each plan file, contradicting
   the rule that additional JSON keys are ignored.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: Take any runnable plan costing at most its published target and add an unused JSON
     key whose string value makes the resulting /app/plans/<morning>.json 5,000,001 bytes. Its
     routes, dispatch cost, and JSON field types remain unchanged; the contract says that key is
     ignored. Flip: tests/test_outputs.py:33 fails the file-size assertion before evaluate can
     check those routes, so a contract-compliant plan loses its runnable and target tests. The
     same flip can be produced with JSON whitespace instead of an extra key. The 5,000,000-byte
     limit appears in neither the instruction nor the candidate-visible README, rules, planner,
     checker, orders, targets, or task configuration.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/dispatch-rules.md:54-60, tests/test_outputs.py:22-36,
     tests/test_outputs.py:41-54

4. [Coherent Contract] MAJOR -- hidden grading semantics
   The verifier adds an undisclosed maximum file size to every required plan JSON, although the
   contract imposes no byte limit and explicitly makes non-route JSON keys irrelevant.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: take any cost-valid plan P for (for example) harbour-lanes and serialize {"routes":
     P["routes"], "padding": "x" * 5000001}. The documented plan schema permits other keys and
     says they are ignored, so the disclosed checker evaluates exactly P's routes and cost. The
     same construction applies to each of the other three required plans. Flip: _plan first
     executes os.path.getsize(path) <= MAX_PLAN_BYTES and rejects this 5,000,001-byte-plus valid
     JSON before json loading or evaluate; therefore the target assertion is never reached and
     the submission fails, whereas the candidate-visible checker would accept P with the
     unchanged cost.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/dispatch-rules.md:54-60, tests/test_outputs.py:30-38,
     tests/test_outputs.py:52-54
submission_document.quality_check_summary:
## Quality Check Results
✅ pass - verifiable: tests/test_outputs.py reads the agent's plan JSON as pure data and evaluates it with a self-contained, deterministic integer-arithmetic function (check_plan.evaluate) against baked copies of orders/targets; no LLM judging, no network, no randomness. test.sh runs pytest once and writes reward from its exit code. This is fully reliable and reproducible across runs.
✅ pass - solvable: solution/solve.sh copies solution/plans/*.json into /app/plans and validates each with the shipped checker; the plan comments (echoed in solve.sh) state the exact costs (77867/147362/201921/288705) matching tests/targets.json exactly, so the shipped solution should pass all eight tests. expert_time_estimate_hours=6 and the described metaheuristic (string-removal + simulated annealing over the rules) is implementable by an OR-competent engineer in a few hours, consistent with the 'few hours at most' bar.
✅ pass - difficult: The task is a heterogeneous-fleet VRPTW with per-kind capacity/pace/shift/range, fixed+variable costs, and limited vehicle counts, requiring a genuine local-search/metaheuristic (not simple greedy/insertion) to beat a tight target. This is squarely in the domain of operations-research/vehicle-routing expertise, well beyond an undergraduate course project.
✅ pass - interesting: Heterogeneous-fleet, time-windowed delivery route optimization with fixed vehicle costs is a real dispatch-planning problem that logistics/OR engineers are paid to solve; the scenario (bakery wholesale deliveries) is a plausible stand-in for real fleet dispatch software.
✅ pass - outcome_verified: Tests only check the resulting /app/plans/<morning>.json files for rule-feasibility and cost vs. target; the instruction explicitly says 'how you produce them is up to you.' No process or tool is mandated.
✅ pass - anti_cheat_robustness: The verifier re-implements the dispatch rules and uses its own baked copies of orders/targets/check_plan.py in the separate verifier image; nothing the agent edits in /app/tools or /app/orders reaches grading, and check_plan.evaluate enforces full feasibility (unique service, windows, capacity, shift, range, fleet counts), preventing trivial shortcuts.
✅ pass - task_security: Both Dockerfiles and all scripts (test.sh, check_plan.py, plan_morning.py, solve.sh) perform only task-scoped, legitimate operations; no exfiltration, obfuscation, or destructive commands were found.
✅ pass - functional_verification: Verification calls evaluate() on parsed JSON data and checks numeric feasibility/cost, not string/keyword matching on the agent's approach or code.
✅ pass - deterministic_reproducible: Distances are computed with integer math (math.isqrt with ceiling), no floating-point or randomness is used in scoring; both Dockerfiles pin base images by digest and pip packages by exact version; no live services are used.
✅ pass - essential_difficulty: The plan JSON schema is minimal (type/depart/stops) and the checker gives precise integer error messages; failures would stem from infeasible or costly routing decisions, not from formatting/precision minutiae.
✅ pass - test_instruction_alignment: The instruction requires, for each of the four named mornings, a plan obeying the dispatch rules and costing at or below the target; the eight tests (one feasibility + one target check per morning) map exactly to that requirement with no extra hidden requirements.
✅ pass - novel: This is a custom-generated VRPTW instance with a bespoke rule set (fixed+variable cost, per-kind pace/shift/range, integer-second departures) that would not appear verbatim in training data; memorized VRP solutions would not transfer to this specific rule combination and data.
✅ pass - agentic: Solving requires exploring the environment (rules doc, orders, checker, baseline planner), writing and iterating a search algorithm across four large instances, and repeatedly invoking the checker — this cannot be done in a single zero-shot generation.
✅ pass - reviewable: A non-specialist reviewer can read dispatch-rules.md (plain-English rules) and the ~80-line check_plan.py, then mechanically run it against the shipped solution/plans/*.json to see the cost exactly matches tests/targets.json, verifying the targets are achievable without needing OR expertise to reproduce the search itself.
✅ pass - instruction_concision: instruction.md is two short paragraphs, uses absolute paths throughout (/app/planner/plan_morning.py, /app/orders/, /app/plans/<morning>.json, /app/docs/dispatch-rules.md, /app/tools/check_plan.py), states the end goal without prescribing an algorithm, and has no headings/roleplay/fluff.
❌ fail - solution_quality: solve.sh only `cp`s precomputed solution/plans/*.json into place and runs the checker; no script that performs the described string-removal/simulated-annealing search is included anywhere in the task tree (only the comments in solve.sh narrate the process). This is a precomputed-artifact use case, but the exception's condition (1) — 'the script that generated the artifact is included in solution/' — is not met, so the solution does not demonstrate genuine computation and is not eligible for the exception.
✅ pass - separate_verifier_configured: The verifier reads only the declared artifact (/app/plans/, matching task.toml's artifacts) plus files baked into tests/Dockerfile (orders, targets.json, check_plan.py); pytest and pytest-json-ctrf are pre-installed in tests/Dockerfile with no runtime installs in test.sh; duplicated assets (check_plan.py, orders/*.json, targets.json) were spot-checked byte-identical between environment/app and tests/ (confirmed at line 2211+ of the largest file, north-ring.json).
✅ pass - environment_hygiene: environment/Dockerfile only COPYs app/ (no tests/ or solution/) and installs generic harness tools (tmux, asciinema, ca-certificates) with proper apt-get update + rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* cleanup; tests/Dockerfile owns pytest/ctrf install and COPYs only its own build context (tests/) into /tests/, with no apt usage needed.
✅ pass - structured_data_schema: dispatch-rules.md gives an explicit, normative JSON schema for a plan ({'routes': [{'type', 'depart', 'stops'}, ...]}) with field semantics (depart must be a JSON integer, stops are customer ids in visit order), not just an example.
✅ pass - typos: No typos were found in filenames, paths, commands, or identifiers across instruction.md, dispatch-rules.md, README.md, Dockerfiles, test files, or solution files during inspection.
❌ fail - difficulty_explanation_quality: The explanation gives good intrinsic-difficulty content (heterogeneous fleet, hard windows, capacity/shift/range, fixed-cost dominance, plateau past simple insertion+relocate heuristics) but explicitly cites experimental results — 'a one-minute insertion plus relocate heuristic lands 13-14 percent above target, and two GPT-5.6 runs with the Codex agent used their full 90 minutes and neither produced runnable plans' — which the guidance explicitly forbids ('Do not mention specific pass rates, benchmark scores, or how particular models performed'). It also omits the required one-sentence note on who would do this work in the real world (that detail lives only in the separate relevant_experience field).
✅ pass - solution_explanation_quality: The solution_explanation clearly summarizes the string-removal + simulated-annealing metaheuristic, the kind-swap/relocation moves, and the departure-time-tightening trick, and correctly states that solve.sh itself just copies the plans and runs the checker — congruent with what solve.sh actually does, even though the generating script is not shipped (a solution_quality issue, not an explanation-quality one).
✅ pass - verification_explanation_quality: The explanation accurately describes that the verifier re-evaluates plans with its own copy of the rules/orders/targets, that no agent code runs, and that each morning has a feasibility test and a target-cost test; it also states the concrete failure modes of the baseline planner, all consistent with test_outputs.py and check_plan.py. The 'no more than target' check is an exact integer inequality against a fixed known-achievable value (the reference plan's own cost), not a fuzzy tolerance needing separate calibration justification.
✅ pass - category_and_tags: category='Operations', subcategory='Logistics' fit a fleet-dispatch VRP task well; tags (vehicle-routing, time-windows, heterogeneous-fleet, metaheuristics, dispatch-planning) are specific and descriptive rather than generic.
✅ pass - no_extraneous_files: Every file present is referenced: environment/app/* is copied by environment/Dockerfile and described in instruction.md/README; solution/plans and solve.sh are used by the reference solution; tests/* are used by tests/Dockerfile and test.sh. No stray or unused files were found.
➖ not_applicable - verifier_execution_isolation: The verifier only parses the agent's plan JSON as data and evaluates it with its own pure-Python function; it never executes, imports, or runs any agent-produced code or binary.
✅ pass - ctrf_reporting: test.sh runs `python3 -I -m pytest ... --ctrf /logs/verifier/ctrf.json /tests/test_outputs.py -rA`, emitting a per-test CTRF report for the eight discrete tests.
➖ not_applicable - do_not_modify_enforced: instruction.md contains no 'do not modify/preserve/leave unchanged' constraint on any concrete artifact; it only says to replace the existing plans, which is the task's whole point.
✅ pass - binary_reward: test.sh only ever writes literal 0 or 1 to /logs/verifier/reward.txt, derived directly from the pytest exit code, with no intermediate fractional scoring path.

## Blocking Quality Gates
✅ PASS - verifiable
✅ PASS - solvable
✅ PASS - outcome_verified
✅ PASS - anti_cheat_robustness
✅ PASS - task_security
✅ PASS - functional_verification
✅ PASS - deterministic_reproducible
✅ PASS - test_instruction_alignment
✅ PASS - agentic
✅ PASS - separate_verifier_configured
✅ PASS - environment_hygiene
✅ PASS - structured_data_schema
✅ PASS - typos
✅ PASS - category_and_tags
✅ PASS - no_extraneous_files
✅ PASS - verifier_execution_isolation
✅ PASS - ctrf_reporting
✅ PASS - do_not_modify_enforced
✅ PASS - binary_reward

## Pre-Difficulty Gate Failed

Difficulty not run: the submission did not pass every blocking quality or quality panel check. Oracle/NOP already passed. No Opus, GPT, analysis, or rubric-generation runs were started.

QUALITY PANEL: NEEDS REVISION -- 3 blocking issues to fix. Details for each are below.

Blocking (fix every one):
   1. [Coherent Contract] MAJOR: The verifier imposes an undisclosed 2,000,000-byte
      schedule-file limit, rejecting valid JSON representations without changing their
      assignments or cost.
   2. [Sound Verifier] MINOR: Ordinary JSON loading erases duplicate press-ID keys, so the
      verifier cannot enforce the rule that each press key occurs at most once.
   3. [Sound Verifier] MINOR: Duplicate press keys in the JSON text are accepted because
      json.load discards all but the last occurrence before the verifier checks press keys.

Checked and clean: Correct Reference Solution, Protected Ground Truth, Deterministic Execution.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DETAILS
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. [Coherent Contract] MAJOR -- hidden grading semantics
   The verifier imposes an undisclosed 2,000,000-byte schedule-file limit, rejecting valid JSON
   representations without changing their assignments or cost.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: The candidate controls /app/schedules/week-36.json, which both week-36 tests read.
     Serialize a feasible week-36 schedule compactly into L bytes and append exactly 2,000,001-L
     ASCII spaces. For example, the shipped planner produces a feasible assignment of the week's
     45 jobs whose compact representation is far below the ceiling; padding this file preserves
     feasibility. For Reviewer 1's construction, the same transformation applies to any
     target-meeting schedule and preserves its target-meeting cost. Flip: At
     tests/test_outputs.py:32 the existing regular file passes isfile; at line 33 getsize
     returns 2,000,001, so the comparison against MAX_BYTES=2,000,000 is false. Execution stops
     before json.load at line 35 and evaluate at line 37. Thus test_week_36_schedule_is_valid
     changes from passing for the compact feasible schedule to failing for the padded
     representation. A target-meeting schedule also loses its target-test pass. In contrast, the

agent_result.text_summary:
## Pre-Difficulty Gate Failed

Difficulty not run: the submission did not pass every blocking quality or quality panel check. Oracle/NOP already passed. No Opus, GPT, analysis, or rubric-generation runs were started.

QUALITY PANEL: NEEDS REVISION -- 1 blocking issue to fix. Details for each are below.

Blocking (fix every one):
   1. [Sound Verifier] MINOR: The schedule decoder accepts nonstandard NaN tokens in ignored
      top-level fields, allowing a non-JSON artifact to pass the required JSON-file validation.

Checked and clean: Coherent Contract, Correct Reference Solution, Protected Ground Truth,
  Deterministic Execution.

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
DETAILS
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. [Sound Verifier] MINOR -- partial output validation
   The schedule decoder accepts nonstandard NaN tokens in ignored top-level fields, allowing a
   non-JSON artifact to pass the required JSON-file validation.
   Why this fails:
     Reach: Take any four target-meeting schedules and add the literal member "diagnostic":NaN
     to each root object, leaving its presses member unchanged. This mutation reaches
     load_schedule through every _cost call at test_outputs.py:33-35. At check_schedule.py:26,
     json.load uses its default parse_constant behavior, decoding NaN to a floating-point NaN
     rather than raising a JSON syntax error. The _Pairs hook retains diagnostic; neither
     duplicate-key check at lines 27-31 rejects the new unique key. evaluate checks the root and
     presses objects at lines 55-56, then iterates only schedule["presses"] at line 60. It never
     reads diagnostic. Thus every assignment, clock, setup total, penalty, and returned integer
     cost C is identical to the original schedule.
     Flip: All four validity tests still succeed, and each target test still evaluates the same
     true inequality C <= T, with T respectively 33983, 47936, 77699, and 112876. Consequently
     pytest exits zero and test.sh:17-18 awards reward 1, whereas a standards-compliant JSON
     loader would reject the mutated artifacts. This is a preservation argument for any passing
     schedules, not a claim that empty or otherwise inadequate schedules pass. The construction
     exploits a narrow decoder extension and still requires solving the scheduling optimization;
     it lies on the deliberate format-bypass side of the reachability distinction, supporting
     Minor.
   Where to look: environment/app/docs/press-rules.md:48-56, tests/check_schedule.py:24-32,
     tests/check_schedule.py:55-60, tests/test_outputs.py:29-42, tests/test.sh:15-20

novel.explanation: While sequence-dependent-setup scheduling is a known research area, this specific synthetic instance (custom die-family setup matrix, per-press maintenance windows, tonnage classes, targets from a bespoke pooled search) is not a memorizable textbook problem; solving it requires genuine search over the given data, not recall.

typos.explanation: No typos found in filenames, paths, identifiers, or prose across instruction.md, task.toml, Dockerfiles, press-rules.md, and the Python sources inspected.

agentic.explanation: The task requires exploring the environment, understanding the rules doc, writing and iterating a search program, running it against a 90-minute budget across four separate instances, and inspecting outputs — this cannot be done as a single zero-shot generation.

solvable.explanation: solution/solve.sh copies solution/schedules/*.json into /app/schedules and runs the shipped checker on each, and the schedules' job-id sets match each week's job list exactly (verified for week-37: 85 job ids in week-37.json match 85 scheduled ids). The search code (lns.py/ils.py) implementing ruin-and-recreate + iterated local search is straightforward for an OR-experienced engineer to write in a few hours, matching expert_time_estimate_hours=6.

difficult.explanation: The task is unrelated-parallel-machine scheduling with sequence-dependent setups, tonnage eligibility, release/due dates, weighted tardiness, and maintenance windows that must not be crossed by any changeover or run — a well-known NP-hard combinatorial optimization class that genuinely requires metaheuristic search (as the provided lns.py/ils.py demonstrate) and OR expertise to approach well; the shipped EDD dispatch baseline costs 2-4x the targets.

reviewable.explanation: The verifier's cost/validity logic is a short, readable simulation directly derived from press-rules.md rather than hardcoded numbers, and solve.sh/solution_explanation lay out how targets were derived (pooled ruin-and-recreate + ILS search), letting a non-specialist reviewer follow the logic even without deep OR background.

verifiable.explanation: tests/test_outputs.py deterministically parses each submitted schedule as data and recomputes cost with the verifier's own copy of check_schedule.py against the verifier's own copy of the week/target data; there is no LLM-as-judge, no randomness, and no runtime network installs (pytest/pytest-json-ctrf are baked into tests/Dockerfile, test.sh only runs pytest).

interesting.explanation: Sequence-dependent-setup parallel-machine scheduling with maintenance windows and weighted tardiness is a standard, paid problem in production/operations-research consulting for stamping/press shops; the task is modeled directly on this real scenario.

binary_reward.explanation: tests/test.sh writes exactly `echo 0` or `echo 1` to /logs/verifier/reward.txt based on the pytest exit code, with no intermediate fractional or weighted value on any path.

task_security.explanation: All Dockerfiles, scripts, and test files perform only legitimate setup/build/verify actions (apt installs of tmux/asciinema/ca-certificates, pinned pip installs, file copies); no exfiltration, obfuscation, destructive commands, or prompt injection found.

ctrf_reporting.explanation: test.sh invokes pytest with `--ctrf /logs/verifier/ctrf.json` against test_outputs.py, producing a per-test CTRF report covering the 8 discrete week/validity/target checks.

outcome_verified.explanation: Instruction states 'how you produce them is up to you' and only specifies the end state (a valid, on-target schedule file per week); tests only check final schedule validity and cost, not method.

solution_quality.explanation: solve.sh copies a precomputed artifact rather than re-running the (expensive, multi-hour, multi-seed) search, but this qualifies under the precomputed-artifact exception: the generating scripts (lns.py, ils.py) are included in solution/search/, solve.sh's header comments document how and roughly how long the artifacts were produced and how to regenerate them, and solve.sh itself re-validates the copied schedules with check_schedule.py before finishing.

category_and_tags.explanation: category='Operations' with subcategory='Supply chain' is a reasonable fit for production/press-shop scheduling, and tags (machine-scheduling, sequence-dependent-setups, weighted-tardiness, metaheuristics, production-planning) are specific and directly descriptive of the task's skills.

environment_hygiene.explanation: environment/Dockerfile only COPYs app/ (excludes tests/ and solution/, also enforced by .dockerignore) and installs only agent-facing apt packages with update+cleanup; tests/Dockerfile owns all test-only deps (pinned pytest/pytest-json-ctrf) baked at build time, not installed in test.sh.

no_extraneous_files.explanation: Every file present is referenced by some part of the pipeline (Dockerfiles, README, solve.sh, tests) or is required scaffolding (task.toml, instruction.md); no leftover, duplicate, or unused files were found in the tree.

essential_difficulty.explanation: Difficulty comes from the combinatorial trade-off between changeover cost and weighted tardiness under maintenance-window constraints, not from output formatting; the required file format is a simple, minimal JSON object with no fussy precision requirements.

anti_cheat_robustness.explanation: Verifier runs in a separate container (environment_mode=separate) using its own baked copies of weeks/*.json, targets.json, and check_schedule.py (all byte-identical to the agent's copies, confirmed by diffing week-36/37/38/39 and targets.json); only /app/schedules/ is pulled in as an artifact, so nothing the agent edits under /app (including targets.json, which it legitimately needs to see) can influence grading, and solution/ is excluded from the agent image via .dockerignore and the Dockerfile's `COPY app/ /app/`.

instruction_concision.explanation: instruction.md is a brief two-paragraph, human-sounding description using absolute paths (/app/planner/plan_week.py, /app/weeks/, /app/schedules/<week>.json, etc.), states the goal without prescribing a method, and includes no unneeded headings or roleplay.

do_not_modify_enforced.explanation: The instruction contains no 'do not modify/preserve' constraint on any concrete artifact — it explicitly says the agent's method is unconstrained ('how you produce them is up to you').

structured_data_schema.explanation: The exact schedule JSON schema (`{"presses": {"P1": [...], ...}}`, key/format rules) is explicitly and normatively specified in the 'File format' section of press-rules.md, which the instruction references directly.

functional_verification.explanation: Verification executes a real discrete-event simulation (evaluate() in check_schedule.py) over the submitted schedule and compares the resulting numeric cost to a target; it never scans source text or keywords.

deterministic_reproducible.explanation: Both Dockerfiles pin the base image by sha256 digest; pip deps in tests/Dockerfile are version-pinned; no live services are used; the simulation and comparison are pure/deterministic given the fixed input files.

test_instruction_alignment.explanation: Instruction requires, for each of the 4 named weeks, a valid schedule at a specific path meeting the target cost; the 8 tests (validity + target-met, per week) test exactly this and nothing more.

separate_verifier_configured.explanation: The verifier only reads the declared artifact (/app/schedules/) plus files baked into /tests/ via `COPY . /tests/`; its own tooling (pytest, pytest-json-ctrf) is pre-installed in tests/Dockerfile with no runtime installs in test.sh; duplicated assets (weeks/*.json, targets.json, check_schedule.py) are verified byte-identical between environment/ and tests/.

solution_explanation_quality.explanation: The solution_explanation concisely and accurately describes the ruin-and-recreate + simulated-annealing search followed by iterated local search, matching what lns.py/ils.py actually implement, and explains why the strategy works (assignment and sequencing must be solved jointly).

verifier_execution_isolation.explanation: The verifier only parses the submitted schedule JSON as data and evaluates it with the verifier's own trusted check_schedule.py; it never executes, imports, or runs any agent-produced code.

✅ pass - verifiable: The verifier (tests/test_outputs.py) reads the agent's schedule JSON as data and re-simulates changeovers, releases, maintenance windows and weighted tardiness with its own copy of check_schedule.py, its own weeks/*.json and targets.json. evaluate() is a pure, deterministic function with no randomness; re-running against a fixed submitted schedule always yields the same cost. ✅ pass - difficult: The task is unrelated-parallel-machine scheduling with sequence-dependent setups, tonnage eligibility, release/due dates, weighted tardiness, and hard maintenance-window constraints across up to 220 jobs on 10 presses. Producing a competitive schedule requires building an assignment+sequencing metaheuristic (large neighborhood search / iterated local search) rather than a simple heuristic; the shipped EDD dispatcher lands 2-4x over target. This is squarely graduate/professional-level operations research, not an undergraduate exercise.
✅ pass - interesting: Sequence-dependent-setup scheduling with weighted tardiness and maintenance windows on parallel presses is a real production-planning problem class; production/OR planners at a stamping plant would genuinely be paid to build exactly this kind of scheduler to replace a naive dispatch rule.
✅ pass - outcome_verified: Instructions specify only the end state (a valid schedule file per press-rules.md costing at or below target) and explicitly say 'how you produce them is up to you.' Tests only check the resulting schedule's feasibility and cost, not any particular algorithm or tool.
✅ pass - anti_cheat_robustness: In separate-verifier mode the agent never sees tests/ or solution/ (ground-truth targets are duplicated into the agent's own weeks/targets.json only because the agent legitimately needs to know its target, per the instructions; it never sees a solved schedule). The verifier runs in its own torn-down-after container, reads the submitted JSON purely as data, and recomputes cost independently, so nothing the agent edits under /app besides the schedule content can influence grading.
✅ pass - task_security: No credential access, network exfiltration, obfuscated code, destructive operations, or prompt injection found in any Dockerfile, script, or data file. ✅ pass - functional_verification: Verification executes an actual discrete-event simulation of changeovers/runs/maintenance and sums real costs (evaluate() in check_schedule.py); it does not grep the schedule file or agent code for keywords or patterns.
✅ pass - deterministic_reproducible: No live services are used; all week/target data is baked into both images; pip deps in tests/Dockerfile are version-pinned (pytest==9.1.1, pytest-json-ctrf==0.5.2); the base image is pinned by sha256 digest. Given a fixed submitted schedule, the verifier's cost computation is deterministic and reproducible across runs.
✅ pass - essential_difficulty: Difficulty comes from the combinatorial trade-off between changeover minimization and weighted-tardiness minimization under maintenance-window timing constraints, not from output formatting; the JSON schedule format is simple and unambiguous, and the checker's error messages are clear.
✅ pass - test_instruction_alignment: The instruction's two requirements (schedule follows press-rules.md, and costs no more than each week's target) map exactly to the two tests per week (_cost validity check and check_target). No additional undisclosed requirements are tested and no instruction requirement is left unchecked.
✅ pass - novel: While unrelated-parallel-machine scheduling with sequence-dependent setups is a studied problem class, the specific bespoke instances (particular setup matrix, presses, maintenance windows, 4 distinct weeks) and hard target thresholds are not something an LLM can recall verbatim; a genuine search must be run against these specific instances.
✅ pass - agentic: Solving requires exploring the environment (reading rules/docs, running the existing planner and checker), writing and iterating a nontrivial search program, and repeatedly invoking it against 4 separate week files, which cannot be done in a single zero-shot generation.
✅ pass - reviewable: press-rules.md fully documents the simulation logic that check_schedule.py implements, and solution/search/lns.py and ils.py are provided so a reviewer can trace exactly how the target costs were derived (not hardcoded), even without deep OR expertise, by reading the straightforward simulation and search code.

No fluff, headings, or roleplay.

✅ pass - anti_cheat_robustness: The verifier runs in a separate container (environment_mode=separate) using its own baked copies of weeks/, targets.json and check_schedule.py from tests/Dockerfile; the agent's own /app/tools/check_schedule.py is a legitimate rules copy (not an answer) and targets.json is intentionally exposed as the numeric bar the agent must beat, not the answer schedule itself. No ground-truth schedule is present in the agent image.
✅ pass - task_security: environment/Dockerfile and tests/Dockerfile only install pinned base images, apt packages (tmux/asciinema/ca-certificates) with proper `apt-get update`+cleanup, and pinned pytest/ctrf via pip; test.sh and test_outputs.py contain only benign JSON reading/simulation logic. No exfiltration, obfuscation, or destructive operations found.
✅ pass - functional_verification: test_outputs.py loads each submitted schedule as data and runs it through a full discrete-event simulation (evaluate()) that recomputes changeovers, run times, maintenance clearance and tardiness penalties to derive an exact cost, then compares it against the numeric target — no string/keyword matching on source code is involved.
✅ pass - deterministic_reproducible: Both Dockerfiles pin the exact same base image digest; pytest and pytest-json-ctrf are version-pinned in tests/Dockerfile; there is no network access at verify time and no live service dependency; the checker is a pure deterministic function of the input JSON, so repeated runs against the same schedule always give the same result.
✅ pass - essential_difficulty: Difficulty stems from genuine combinatorial reasoning (assignment + sequencing under sequence-dependent setups, tonnage constraints, and maintenance-window timing effects), not from clerical output formatting; the required schedule format is a simple, clearly specified JSON object with no arbitrary precision or exotic formatting requirements.
✅ pass - test_instruction_alignment: The instruction requires, for each of the four named weeks, a schedule at /app/schedules/<week>.json that follows press-rules.md and costs no more than the week's target; the eight tests in test_outputs.py exactly cover this (one validity check + one cost-vs-target check per week), with no extra untested requirements or unrequested checks.
✅ pass - novel: This is a bespoke, custom-authored scheduling instance (synthetic die families, changeover matrix, per-press maintenance windows, weighted tardiness) rather than a canonical textbook algorithm (e.g., sorting, TSP, sudoku); it cannot be solved by pattern-matching against widely available reference solutions.
✅ pass - agentic: Solving requires exploring the repo (docs, tools, weeks), writing and iterating a search program, repeatedly invoking the checker to measure progress, and refining across four distinct problem instances — this cannot be done via a single zero-shot generation.
✅ pass - reviewable: The rules (press-rules.md) and checker (check_schedule.py) are short, explicit, and auditable by a non-specialist; the numeric targets are explicitly derived from included search scripts (solution/search/lns.py, ils.py) rather than being unexplained hardcoded numbers, and the process used to obtain them is documented in solution_explanation.
✅ pass - instruction_concision: instruction.md is two short paragraphs, uses absolute paths (/app/planner/plan_week.py, /app/weeks/, /app/schedules/) throughout, contains no headings, roleplay, or step-by-step procedure, and does not hint at a specific solution algorithm.
✅ pass - solution_quality: solve.sh copies precomputed schedules and re-validates them with the checker; the actual generation code (ruin-and-recreate LNS with simulated annealing, then iterated local search) is included in solution/search/ as real, executable computation, and solve.sh/solution_explanation document provenance (multi-seed, multi-round process, runtimes, regeneration path) — satisfying the precomputed-artifact exception since re-running the full multi-round search on every CI trial would be prohibitively expensive; large logic lives in separate files (lns.py, ils.py) rather than heredocs in solve.sh.
✅ pass - separate_verifier_configured: The verifier only reads /app/schedules (the declared artifact) plus its own baked weeks/targets/check_schedule.py copies from tests/Dockerfile; pytest and pytest-json-ctrf are pre-installed in tests/Dockerfile rather than at verify time; the duplicated weeks/targets/check_schedule.py files are byte- and line-identical between environment/app and tests/.
✅ pass - environment_hygiene: environment/.dockerignore excludes tests/ and solution/ from the agent build context, and environment/Dockerfile only COPYs app/; test-only deps (pytest, pytest-json-ctrf) live solely in tests/Dockerfile; apt installs in environment/Dockerfile are unpinned with update+cleanup as required; tests/Dockerfile uses no apt at all.
✅ pass - structured_data_schema: press-rules.md's 'File format' section gives an explicit normative JSON schema for the schedule output (`{"presses": {...}}`, key uniqueness rules, job-id string requirements), not just an example.
✅ pass - typos: No typos were found in filenames, paths, variable names, or prose across instruction.md, task.toml, press-rules.md, README.md, or the Python source files inspected.
✅ pass - difficulty_explanation_quality: difficulty_explanation clearly identifies the core tension (changeover savings vs. tardiness, non-local knock-on effects of maintenance windows), quantifies the gap vs. a naive dispatcher, states the data is synthetic-but-realistic (family counts, changeover ranges, press tonnages/stroke rates), and implies the real-world persona (a production planner) — covering both algorithmic/agent difficulty and human domain difficulty without citing benchmark pass rates.
✅ pass - solution_explanation_quality: solution_explanation concretely describes the ruin-and-recreate/simulated-annealing and iterated-local-search strategy, the neighborhood operators used, and how the two scripts (lns.py, ils.py) relate to the shipped solution files — congruent with the actual code in solution/search/.
✅ pass - verification_explanation_quality: verification_explanation accurately describes that the verifier uses its own copies of rules/weeks/targets, checks validity and an exact-cost <= target threshold (not a fuzzy tolerance needing calibration), and gives concrete supporting numbers (reference costs vs. shipped-planner costs) that match test_outputs.py's actual behavior.
✅ pass - category_and_tags: category='Operations' correctly reflects a production/scheduling problem; subcategory='Supply chain' is a reasonable if slightly loose fit (a subcategory like 'production scheduling' might fit marginally better, but Supply chain is defensible for a shop-floor planning task); tags (machine-scheduling, sequence-dependent-setups, weighted-tardiness, metaheuristics, production-planning) are specific and directly descriptive of the task's techniques and domain.
✅ pass - no_extraneous_files: Every file inventoried (task.toml, instruction.md, environment/*, tests/*, solution/*) is referenced by a Dockerfile, the instruction, solve.sh, or the test harness; no editor cruft, backups, or unused assets were found.
➖ not_applicable - verifier_execution_isolation: The verifier never executes or imports agent-produced code; test_outputs.py explicitly loads the submitted schedule JSON as pure data and evaluates it with the verifier's own check_schedule.py, as stated in its own docstring ('no code from /app runs').
✅ pass - ctrf_reporting: test.sh invokes `python3 -I -m pytest ... --ctrf /logs/verifier/ctrf.json /tests/test_outputs.py -rA`, emitting a per-test CTRF report to the standard collected location.
➖ not_applicable - do_not_modify_enforced: instruction.md contains no 'do not modify/preserve/leave unchanged' constraint on any concrete artifact; the agent is free to modify anything in /app, including its local copy of check_schedule.py, without consequence since the verifier uses its own independent copy.
✅ pass - binary_reward: test.sh only ever writes literal `0` or `1` to /logs/verifier/reward.txt (initialized to 0, then set based solely on pytest's exit code with a simple if/else) — no fractional or weighted computation reaches the reward file.

novel.explanation: This is not a standard textbook exercise; it is a bespoke synthetic instance combining unrelated-machine assignment, sequence-dependent setups, weighted tardiness, tonnage eligibility, and maintenance-window blocking simultaneously — a combination unlikely to appear verbatim in training data, requiring genuine search/design rather than recall.

typos.explanation: No typos were found in filenames, paths, commands, or identifiers across instruction.md, task.toml, Dockerfiles, and the Python scripts inspected; code and prose read cleanly.

agentic.explanation: Solving requires exploring the environment, writing and iterating a nontrivial search program, running it for a substantial wall-clock time, checking intermediate results with check_schedule.py, and refining across four separate week instances — this cannot be done in a single zero-shot generation.

solvable.explanation: solution/solve.sh copies solution/schedules/*.json (produced by solution/search/lns.py + ils.py) and runs check_schedule.py on each, which the metadata states passes all four targets (33983/47936/77699/112876 vs targets 36021/50812/82360/119648). The search scripts are genuine, working metaheuristics (ruin-and-recreate + iterated local search) an OR-savvy engineer could implement in a few hours; the metadata documents a fresh one-session run (100 min/week on one core) also beating every target, well inside the agent's 4-hour/2-core budget, demonstrating feasibility without unreasonable effort.

difficult.explanation: The task combines unrelated parallel-machine scheduling, sequence-dependent die-family setups, tonnage eligibility, release times, weighted tardiness, and maintenance windows that block both changeovers and runs. This is a well-known NP-hard combinatorial optimization class requiring metaheuristic design (LNS/ILS, simulated annealing, block moves) to beat a 6%-above-best target; the shipped EDD dispatch planner misses targets by 2-4x, showing naive approaches fail. This plausibly exceeds a typical undergraduate course project and requires genuine OR/metaheuristics expertise to tune within the time budget.

reviewable.explanation: press-rules.md fully specifies the simulation semantics in plain language, and check_schedule.py's evaluate()/clear_of() functions directly mirror that spec, so a non-specialist reviewer can trace the rules to the code. Reference schedules are derived from included search scripts (lns.py/ils.py) rather than hardcoded, and provenance/timing is documented in solution_explanation.

verifiable.explanation: test.sh runs pytest against tests/test_outputs.py, which loads the agent's schedule JSON as pure data and evaluates it with the verifier's own (baked-in) copy of check_schedule.py against the verifier's own copies of week/target data. The evaluate() function is a deterministic pure-Python simulation (no floating point, no randomness), so re-running is guaranteed to produce the same result every time. No runtime network installs occur in test.sh; all verifier deps (pytest, pytest-json-ctrf) are baked into tests/Dockerfile.

interesting.explanation: Production scheduling with sequence-dependent changeovers, weighted tardiness, and maintenance windows is a real job-shop/press-shop planning problem that production planners and operations-research consultants are paid to solve; the task's framing (stamping line, die families, tonnage classes) mirrors real manufacturing scheduling practice.

binary_reward.explanation: test.sh initializes reward.txt to 0, then writes exactly 1 on pytest exit code 0 or 0 otherwise — every reachable path writes exactly 0 or 1, with no fractional or weighted scoring anywhere in the verifier.

task_security.explanation: All files (Dockerfiles, Python scripts, instruction, test harness) perform only legitimate scheduling/verification logic; no exfiltration, obfuscation, destructive commands, or prompt injection was found in any inspected file.

ctrf_reporting.explanation: test.sh runs pytest with '--ctrf /logs/verifier/ctrf.json' against tests/test_outputs.py, matching the recommended pattern and giving per-test (per-week validity/target) granularity.

outcome_verified.explanation: Instructions describe only the end state (produce valid schedules at or under the target cost) and explicitly say 'how you produce them is up to you.' Tests check only the final schedule files' validity and cost, not the process used to generate them.

solution_quality.explanation: The reference schedules are produced by genuine search code (lns.py ruin-and-recreate with simulated annealing, ils.py exhaustive local search) included in solution/search/, not hardcoded; solve.sh documents provenance (search algorithm, runtime, one-session verification) and copies the generated artifacts per the precomputed-artifact exception, since re-running the multi-hour search on every CI/oracle invocation would be prohibitively expensive. Large search scripts are kept as separate files, not heredocs in solve.sh.

environment_hygiene.explanation: environment/Dockerfile only COPYs app/ (excluding tests/ and solution/ via .dockerignore) and installs only generic agent tooling (tmux, asciinema, ca-certificates) with proper apt-get update/cleanup and no version pinning of apt packages. tests/Dockerfile owns all test-only Python deps (pinned pip installs) and creates artifact directories, with no apt usage needing cleanup.

no_extraneous_files.explanation: Every file inventoried (Dockerfiles, docs, weeks/targets data, planner/checker scripts, solution search scripts and schedules, tests) is referenced by either a Dockerfile COPY, the instruction, solve.sh, or the test harness; no editor cruft, backups, or unused assets were found.

essential_difficulty.explanation: The required output format is a simple {'presses': {id: [job_ids]}} JSON structure with minimal formatting burden; the actual difficulty comes from the underlying combinatorial optimization (assignment + sequencing under multiple constraints), not from clerical output formatting.

anti_cheat_robustness.explanation: solution/ and tests/ are excluded from the agent image via environment/.dockerignore and by the Dockerfile only copying app/; the reference/best schedules and one-session artifacts never reach the agent container. The verifier runs in a separate container using its own baked-in copies of check_schedule.py, week data, and targets, so nothing the agent writes to /app (other than the declared schedule artifacts) can influence grading.

instruction_concision.explanation: The instruction is short, uses absolute paths (/app/planner/plan_week.py, /app/schedules/<week>.json, etc.), states the goal upfront, and explicitly leaves the approach open ('how you produce them is up to you') without prescribing an algorithm or step-by-step procedure.

do_not_modify_enforced.explanation: instruction.md contains no 'do not modify / preserve' constraint naming a concrete artifact; the agent is free to write only the four schedule files, so there is no such constraint to enforce.

structured_data_schema.explanation: The exact JSON schema for the schedule output is normatively specified in the 'File format' section of press-rules.md ({'presses': {pressId: [jobId,...]}}), which the instruction explicitly references.

functional_verification.explanation: Verification executes check_schedule.py's evaluate() function against the submitted schedule's actual job placements, timings, and costs — a full simulation of changeovers, releases, and maintenance windows — rather than any string/keyword matching on submitted files.

deterministic_reproducible.explanation: The base image is pinned by SHA256 digest in both Dockerfiles, verifier Python deps are pinned exact versions (pytest==9.1.1, pytest-json-ctrf==0.5.2), there is no live-service dependency, and the cost simulation is pure integer/deterministic arithmetic with no randomness at verify time.

test_instruction_alignment.explanation: The instruction requires four schedule files at /app/schedules/<week>.json that follow press-rules.md and meet each week's target; test_outputs.py has exactly one validity test and one target-cost test per week, tracing directly to those two requirements with no extra checks beyond what's described.

separate_verifier_configured.explanation: Verifier reads only /app/schedules (declared in artifacts), and tests/Dockerfile pre-installs pytest and pytest-json-ctrf so test.sh performs no runtime installs. Shared assets (check_schedule.py, weeks/*.json, targets.json) are byte-identical between environment/app, solution/search, and tests, and the same pinned base-image digest is used in both Dockerfiles.

solution_explanation_quality.explanation: The solution_explanation describes the two-stage metaheuristic (LNS with annealing, then ILS with exhaustive relocation/swap/block moves), explains the multi-seed pooling used for the reference numbers, and gives concrete empirical evidence (one-session timings and resulting costs) that is consistent with lns.py/ils.py as actually implemented.

verifier_execution_isolation.explanation: The verifier never executes agent-produced code; it only parses the agent's schedule JSON as data and evaluates it with the verifier's own trusted check_schedule.py running entirely in the root pytest process, so this criterion does not apply.

difficulty_explanation_quality.explanation: The difficulty_explanation clearly identifies the core tension (changeover savings vs. tardiness, maintenance windows causing knock-on delays), names who would do this in reality ('a production planner has to build a search...'), states the data is synthetic but modelled on a real stamping line, and avoids mentioning any pass-rate/benchmark figures.

verification_explanation_quality.explanation: The verification_explanation accurately describes that the verifier re-simulates each schedule with its own rules/data and checks validity plus cost <= target, matching test_outputs.py exactly; it also reports the shipped planner's costs against targets, giving concrete calibration evidence that the threshold is meaningfully tight yet reachable (validated by an independent one-session search run, not just the reference solution).

novel.explanation: This is a custom-generated VRPTW instance with a bespoke rule set (fixed+variable cost, per-kind pace/shift/range, integer-second departures) that would not appear verbatim in training data; memorized VRP solutions would not transfer to this specific rule combination and data.

typos.explanation: No typos were found in filenames, paths, commands, or identifiers across instruction.md, dispatch-rules.md, README.md, Dockerfiles, test files, or solution files during inspection.

agentic.explanation: Solving requires exploring the environment (rules doc, orders, checker, baseline planner), writing and iterating a search algorithm across four large instances, and repeatedly invoking the checker — this cannot be done in a single zero-shot generation.

solvable.explanation: solution/solve.sh copies solution/plans/*.json into /app/plans and validates each with the shipped checker; the plan comments (echoed in solve.sh) state the exact costs (77867/147362/201921/288705) matching tests/targets.json exactly, so the shipped solution should pass all eight tests. expert_time_estimate_hours=6 and the described metaheuristic (string-removal + simulated annealing over the rules) is implementable by an OR-competent engineer in a few hours, consistent with the 'few hours at most' bar.

difficult.explanation: The task is a heterogeneous-fleet VRPTW with per-kind capacity/pace/shift/range, fixed+variable costs, and limited vehicle counts, requiring a genuine local-search/metaheuristic (not simple greedy/insertion) to beat a tight target. This is squarely in the domain of operations-research/vehicle-routing expertise, well beyond an undergraduate course project.

reviewable.explanation: A non-specialist reviewer can read dispatch-rules.md (plain-English rules) and the ~80-line check_plan.py, then mechanically run it against the shipped solution/plans/*.json to see the cost exactly matches tests/targets.json, verifying the targets are achievable without needing OR expertise to reproduce the search itself.

verifiable.explanation: tests/test_outputs.py reads the agent's plan JSON as pure data and evaluates it with a self-contained, deterministic integer-arithmetic function (check_plan.evaluate) against baked copies of orders/targets; no LLM judging, no network, no randomness. test.sh runs pytest once and writes reward from its exit code. This is fully reliable and reproducible across runs.

interesting.explanation: Heterogeneous-fleet, time-windowed delivery route optimization with fixed vehicle costs is a real dispatch-planning problem that logistics/OR engineers are paid to solve; the scenario (bakery wholesale deliveries) is a plausible stand-in for real fleet dispatch software.

binary_reward.explanation: test.sh only ever writes literal 0 or 1 to /logs/verifier/reward.txt, derived directly from the pytest exit code, with no intermediate fractional scoring path.

task_security.explanation: Both Dockerfiles and all scripts (test.sh, check_plan.py, plan_morning.py, solve.sh) perform only task-scoped, legitimate operations; no exfiltration, obfuscation, or destructive commands were found.

ctrf_reporting.explanation: test.sh runs `python3 -I -m pytest ... --ctrf /logs/verifier/ctrf.json /tests/test_outputs.py -rA`, emitting a per-test CTRF report for the eight discrete tests.

outcome_verified.explanation: Tests only check the resulting /app/plans/<morning>.json files for rule-feasibility and cost vs. target; the instruction explicitly says 'how you produce them is up to you.' No process or tool is mandated.

solution_quality.explanation: solve.sh only `cp`s precomputed solution/plans/*.json into place and runs the checker; no script that performs the described string-removal/simulated-annealing search is included anywhere in the task tree (only the comments in solve.sh narrate the process). This is a precomputed-artifact use case, but the exception's condition (1) — 'the script that generated the artifact is included in solution/' — is not met, so the solution does not demonstrate genuine computation and is not eligible for the exception.

category_and_tags.explanation: category='Operations', subcategory='Logistics' fit a fleet-dispatch VRP task well; tags (vehicle-routing, time-windows, heterogeneous-fleet, metaheuristics, dispatch-planning) are specific and descriptive rather than generic.

environment_hygiene.explanation: environment/Dockerfile only COPYs app/ (no tests/ or solution/) and installs generic harness tools (tmux, asciinema, ca-certificates) with proper apt-get update + rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* cleanup; tests/Dockerfile owns pytest/ctrf install and COPYs only its own build context (tests/) into /tests/, with no apt usage needed.

anti_cheat_robustness.explanation: The verifier re-implements the dispatch rules and uses its own baked copies of orders/targets/check_plan.py in the separate verifier image; nothing the agent edits in /app/tools or /app/orders reaches grading, and check_plan.evaluate enforces full feasibility (unique service, windows, capacity, shift, range, fleet counts), preventing trivial shortcuts.

structured_data_schema.explanation: dispatch-rules.md gives an explicit, normative JSON schema for a plan ({'routes': [{'type', 'depart', 'stops'}, ...]}) with field semantics (depart must be a JSON integer, stops are customer ids in visit order), not just an example.

separate_verifier_configured.explanation: The verifier reads only the declared artifact (/app/plans/, matching task.toml's artifacts) plus files baked into tests/Dockerfile (orders, targets.json, check_plan.py); pytest and pytest-json-ctrf are pre-installed in tests/Dockerfile with no runtime installs in test.sh; duplicated assets (check_plan.py, orders/*.json, targets.json) were spot-checked byte-identical between environment/app and tests/ (confirmed at line 2211+ of the largest file, north-ring.json).

solution_explanation_quality.explanation: The solution_explanation clearly summarizes the string-removal + simulated-annealing metaheuristic, the kind-swap/relocation moves, and the departure-time-tightening trick, and correctly states that solve.sh itself just copies the plans and runs the checker — congruent with what solve.sh actually does, even though the generating script is not shipped (a solution_quality issue, not an explanation-quality one).

verifier_execution_isolation.explanation: The verifier only parses the agent's plan JSON as data and evaluates it with its own pure-Python function; it never executes, imports, or runs any agent-produced code or binary.

difficulty_explanation_quality.explanation: The explanation gives good intrinsic-difficulty content (heterogeneous fleet, hard windows, capacity/shift/range, fixed-cost dominance, plateau past simple insertion+relocate heuristics) but explicitly cites experimental results — 'a one-minute insertion plus relocate heuristic lands 13-14 percent above target, and two GPT-5.6 runs with the Codex agent used their full 90 minutes and neither produced runnable plans' — which the guidance explicitly forbids ('Do not mention specific pass rates, benchmark scores, or how particular models performed'). It also omits the required one-sentence note on who would do this work in the real world (that detail lives only in the separate relevant_experience field).

verification_explanation_quality.explanation: The explanation accurately describes that the verifier re-evaluates plans with its own copy of the rules/orders/targets, that no agent code runs, and that each morning has a feasibility test and a target-cost test; it also states the concrete failure modes of the baseline planner, all consistent with test_outputs.py and check_plan.py. The 'no more than target' check is an exact integer inequality against a fixed known-achievable value (the reference plan's own cost), not a fuzzy tolerance needing separate calibration justification.

fields.label: Quality Judge Panel Feedback
fields.description:
After initial submission, you will be provided with detailed feedback along 5 axes, each answering a core question about your task:

  1. Coherent Contracts: Can a candidate determine every rule used to grade the task?
  2. Correct Reference Solution: Does the reference satisfy the documented task?
  3. Protected Ground Truth: Can candidate code obtain or control the answer the grader trusts?
  4. Sound Verifier: Does grading reject wrong solutions and accept contract-valid ones?
  5. Deterministic Execution: Does the same submission receive stable grading on repeated runs?

Keep these in mind when reviewing this feedback, and refer to the guidelines for more details on this feedback.
